name: Nasal
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Hakim, Jacob Abadir. 2024. A prosodic description of Nasal: investigating stress and intonation in an endangered Sumatran language. PhD dissertation, University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa (Linguistics), December 2024. 397 pp.https://hdl.handle.net/10125/110195(ScholarSpace, open access)
catalog_locator: Ch. 4 §4.4 Discussion, p. 174; Ch. 10 §10.1 'Answering the research questions', Question 1, p. 327. Supporting: §3.1.5 p. 84; §4.1 p. 98; §4.5 p. 174; §10.1 p. 328; §10.2.1 p. 330.
catalog_quote: Yes, it is true that ultimas in Nasal words are longer than penults. But in the absence of other evidence, the findings of these analyses lead me to conclude that there is no reason to treat Nasal as having consistent word-level stress. [p. 174] ... Based on the analysis of acoustic patterns at the lexical (and post-lexical) level presented in Chapter 4, there does not appear to be any evidence for a consistent pattern of word-level stress in Nasal. This was demonstrated through statistical modeling of acoustic properties such as F0, duration, intensity, vowel quality and spectral tilt across different syllable positions. Where significant differences in syllable position did exist, they did not align on a certain syllable, with some cues (e.g. duration) generally more prominent on the final syllable, and others (e.g. spectral tilt) generally more prominent on the penultimate syllable. ... Therefore, even if it might be argued that there are certain regular rhythmic properties of Nasal word prosody, such as slightly longer final syllables, this cannot be argued to constitute 'stress' in the sense that this phenomenon is discussed in other languages, since both lexical and post-lexical acoustic properties fail to converge in a way that would constitute phonologically meaningful, regular prosodic prominence. [p. 327]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nasal has no word-level stress. An acoustic experiment (duration, F0, intensity, vowel quality, spectral tilt across penult vs. final syllable, mixed-effects models, mirror-word stimuli) found only slight, non-converging effects: final syllables somewhat longer and with slight vowel-height differences, penults slightly favoured by F0 and spectral tilt; speakers have no intuitions about a stressed syllable. The author analyses Nasal as a stressless, head-marking intonation language: prominence is assigned post-lexically as pitch accents (most often realised on the penultimate syllable of the focused or phrase-final word) plus complex right-edge boundary tones, with strong lengthening of IP-final ultimas.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not applicable; none posited (no word stress at all).
new_statements.exceptions: Ultimas are consistently slightly longer than penults (a rhythmic tendency the author declines to call stress); prominence at the phrase level can land on penult or ultima of the same word for different speakers; utterance-final words are strongly lengthened to carry boundary-tone targets. Impressionistic pilot (p. 84): 'there did not appear to be any predictable stress patterns'.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about word-level (lexical) stress, tested on disyllabic target words in carrier sentences (medial vs. final position, focus manipulated) and in read dialogues; phrase-level prominence (pitch accents, boundary tones) is described separately and is where all prominence is assigned.
new_statements.identity_note: Hakim 2024 describes the Nasal language of Kaur Regency, Bengkulu (ISO nsy, Glottolog nasa1239), with speakers from Nasal villages (fieldwork based in Gedung Menung); no dialect split is discussed and the earlier survey (Anderbeck & Aprilani 2013) treats Nasal as a single variety. Not to be confused with the English word 'nasal'.

sources.note: Whole dissertation is on prosody; ch. 3 gives a phonology sketch, ch. 4 is an acoustic experiment 'Searching for stress' (duration, F0, intensity, vowel quality, spectral tilt, mixed models); concludes there is no convincing/compelling evidence for word-level stress in Nasal; the language is analysed as a stressless head-marking language with post-lexical pitch accents (tending to the penult of the focused/phrase-final word) and complex right-edge boundary tones.
